questions.question: What is the difference between map, forEach and filter? Which one do you reach for when you need to remove items?
questions.answer: All three loop over an array and run a callback, but their contracts differ. map transforms every element and returns a new array of the same length — one output per input. forEach runs a side effect and returns undefined, so it cannot be chained; it is for logging, DOM writes or pushing into another array. filter returns a new array containing only the elements whose callback returned truthy, so it can shrink the array (and may return an empty one). To remove items you use filter; to reshape items you use map; to accumulate into a single value you use reduce. A common mistake is calling map when the callback returns nothing useful, or calling forEach and then wondering why the result is undefined.
key_points: map: same length, new array, chainable
forEach: returns undefined, meant for side effects
filter: keeps truthy results, new (possibly empty) array
Use filter to remove, map to reshape, reduce to accumulate

questions.answer:
It prints [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ], then [ 1, NaN, NaN ], then [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ].

sort() without a comparator converts each element to a string and compares lexicographically, so "10" comes before "9" because "1" < "9". It also mutates in place and returns the same array, so the third line shows the reordered original. The fix is nums.sort((a, b) => a - b).

The second line is the map(parseInt) trap: map calls the callback with (element, index, array), and parseInt takes (string, radix). So it evaluates parseInt(1, 0) = 1, parseInt(2, 1) = NaN (radix 1 is invalid), parseInt(3, 2) = NaN (binary has no digit 3). The fix is to wrap it: [1, 2, 3].map((n) => parseInt(n, 10)).
key_points: Default sort compares strings, so 10 sorts before 9
sort mutates and returns the same array
Numeric sort: sort((a, b) => a - b)
map passes (element, index, array); the index becomes parseInt's radix
Wrap callbacks that take extra arguments

questions.question: Write unique(arr) that removes duplicates while preserving first-seen order, and works for objects by reference and for NaN.
questions.answer:
const unique = (arr) => [...new Set(arr)];

console.log(unique([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])); // [ 3, 1, 2 ]
console.log(unique([NaN, NaN, 1]));   // [ NaN, 1 ]

Set uses SameValueZero for key equality: insertion order is preserved, NaN equals NaN, and objects are compared by reference (two structurally equal objects stay distinct). Spreading the Set back into an array is the idiomatic ES6+ one-liner. If you needed to dedupe objects by a field, you would reduce into a Map keyed by that field instead.
key_points: new Set(arr) dedupes in O(n) and preserves insertion order
Set uses SameValueZero, so NaN is deduped
Objects are compared by reference, not by shape
Spread back to an array: [...new Set(arr)]

Guard size < 1 to avoid an infinite loop
Alternative: Array.from with a mapper over the chunk count

questions.answer:
Output: [ 'Tue', 'Wed' ], then [ 'Mon', 'Thu' ], then [ 'Tue' ], then the original [ 'Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu' ].

splice(start, deleteCount) changes the array in place and returns an array of the removed elements. Starting at index 1 and deleting 2 removes Tue and Wed, leaving Mon and Thu.

slice(start, end) copies a range and returns it, leaving the original untouched. The end index is exclusive, so slice(1, 2) returns only the element at index 1 — one item, not two. The similar names and the fact that one end index is a count while the other is a position is exactly what interviewers test. If you want to remove two items without mutation, use toSpliced(1, 2).
key_points: splice mutates and returns the removed elements
slice copies and returns a new array
splice's second argument is a delete count; slice's is an exclusive end index
toSpliced is the non-mutating ES2023 version

questions.question: Explain reduce's accumulator and initial value. What happens without an initial value, and why is passing one usually the right call?
questions.answer:
reduce(callback, initialValue) walks the array carrying an accumulator. On each step the callback receives (accumulator, current, index, array) and whatever it returns becomes the next accumulator; the final accumulator is the result. If you pass an initial value, the accumulator starts there and the callback runs once per element, including on an empty array (which returns the initial value). If you omit it, the first element becomes the initial accumulator, iteration starts at index 1, and an empty array throws TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value.

Passing an initial value is safer and clearer: the result type is fixed (0 for a sum, {} for grouping, [] for a list), the empty-array case is defined, and the callback does not need to special-case the first element. It also avoids surprises with object arrays, where the accumulator would otherwise start as an object rather than your intended shape.
key_points: Callback gets (accumulator, current, index, array)
Return value becomes the next accumulator; final value is returned
Without an initial value the first element seeds it and empty arrays throw
Always pass 0, {}, [] or the correct starting shape

questions.answer:
new Array(3).map(...) produces [ <3 empty items> ]. Array(3) creates three holes, not three undefineds, and map/filter/forEach skip holes entirely — the callback is never called, so there is nothing to double. The fix is Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i * 2), which calls the mapper for every index and returns [0, 2, 4]; or new Array(3).fill(0).map(...).

[].every(...) is true because of vacuous truth: every element satisfies the predicate, and there are no elements to violate it. Its counterpart [].some(...) is false — no element satisfies it. Because filter and map preserve holes while spread ([...a]) and for...of read them as undefined, sparse arrays behave inconsistently across methods and are best avoided.
key_points: Array(3) creates holes, not undefined values
map/filter/forEach skip holes; Array.from and spread do not
Array.from({ length: n }, mapper) fills correctly
every on [] is true (vacuous); some on [] is false
